question: to the Commission Yannis Maniatis (S&D) Subject:

The Greek Government recently decided to drastically shorten the deadline (from 31 August to 2 June) for signing the loan contracts under the My Home II programme funded by the Recovery Fund. This is despite the fact that, according to the government, there are still EUR 380 million worth of unallocated funds available for the thousands of remaining applicants and many fellow citizens have invested a great deal of time and money in applying for the programme and risk being shut out at the last minute. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Has it agreed to the programme ending early, creating legal uncertainty for citizens and making the EU’s housing policy appear unreliable, when housing is a priority under its current mandate?

Have the consequences been assessed for the thousands of citizens who put their faith in the credibility the EU brought to the programme and who have already advanced money and gone through a number of lengthy and costly preparatory procedures, such as technical/legal checks, regularisation of building irregularities, issuing of required certificates?

Has it assessed whether the My Home I and II programmes – instead of representing policies for the development of public land and vacant housing, the creation of social housing and more generally increasing the housing supply – are in fact effective and do not lead to market distortions, such as a faster increase in the prices of old properties?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) The ‘My Home II’ programme was designed to provide affordable financing for low-income first-time home buyers with little or no access to mortgage lending at lower than market interest rates. The Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP)1 allocates EUR 1 billion to the ‘My Home II’ Facility (ID 16400). While ‘My Home II’ is supporting low-income households facing high housing costs and exhibits positive welfare effects, complementary measures in the Greek RRP aim to address elevated house price growth. In this respect, the Greek RRP also includes the adoption of the national housing strategy and the social exchange programme (Koinoniki Antiparochi). The former includes an analysis of the functioning of the housing market, which should set the ground for effective policies in the area of housing in Greece, while the latter’s goal is to directly increase the supply of affordable housing. The Recovery and Resilience Facility Regulation2 provides that all milestones and targets for the implementation of reforms and investments must be completed by 31 August 2026. As such, all payment requests, including supporting evidence necessary for the Commission’s assessment, must be submitted to the Commission by 30 September 2026. In light of these deadlines, it is the responsibility of the Greek authorities to put in place the necessary arrangements, including the signature of financing agreements with final beneficiaries, ensuring that all the relevant evidence demonstrating the fulfilment of the relevant milestones and targets is timely submitted to the Commission.

and-resilience-plan_en. 2 Regulation (EU) 2021/241 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 February 2021 establishing the Recovery and Resilience Facility: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2021/241/oj/eng.
